name: Jackson v. City of Bremerton
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Western District of Washington, District Judge Robert J. Bryan)
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, chemical irritant sprayed on a woman who ran to interfere with an officer during a melee at a park after a warning to disperse, push to the ground during handcuffing, no constitutional violation found, summary judgment for officers and city affirmed
summary: Outnumbered officers trying to arrest a man on a warrant at a park gathering of thirty to fifty people faced a crowd that shouted, swore, advanced on them and fought. After police warned everyone that a chemical irritant would be used if they did not disperse, a woman ran to interfere with an officer who was fighting a teenager and was sprayed in the hair, then pushed the rest of the way to the ground while being handcuffed. The Ninth Circuit held that the intrusions were minimal, that her active interference posed an immediate threat to the officers' safety and control of a rapidly evolving scene, and that the force was reasonable, so there was no constitutional violation and no municipal liability. It is the counterpoint to Headwaters: chemical agents on a person actively interfering in a melee, after a warning.
coverage: The opinion by Judge Tallman, including all footnotes, was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/268/268.F3d.646.99-36159.html. The archive heads the file 268 F.3d 646 (9th Cir. 2001), No. 99-36159, submitted August 7, 2001 without oral argument, filed October 5, 2001, which confirms the citation.

The archive text has paragraph numbers but no Federal Reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given. The opinion predates the Ninth Circuit's online archive coverage for this docket and was not available there.

The opinion describes the warrant for Jackson's son both as a robbery warrant arising from a felony charge reduced to a misdemeanor theft conviction and, in the analysis, as an outstanding felony warrant. The brief reports both descriptions as the court gave them.

The course materials describe the result as qualified immunity granted. The court's holding is that no Fourth Amendment violation occurred; it addressed qualified immunity only in a footnote as an alternative ground. The brief reports that distinction.
facts:
The court viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to Jackson, the party opposing summary judgment, and relied heavily on her own deposition testimony.

On July 13, 1996, Jeannine Jackson and thirty to fifty friends and family members were gathered at a public park in Bremerton, Washington. Two bicycle officers responded to a report that the group was drinking in the park. One recognized Jackson's adult son, Kevin Blake, from prior contacts and learned he had an outstanding warrant, which the court described as a robbery warrant arising from his failure to make payments on a felony charge that had been reduced to a misdemeanor theft conviction. Because Blake had caused problems for arresting officers before, the officer called for backup.

Told of the warrant, Blake said to speak with his mother, who argued with the officers about it. Blake ran into the crowd and tried to run out of the park, and several friends tried to shield him. More backup was called. After two more officers arrived, Jackson was told one of them had reached for his gun, and she yelled at him about it. As officers worked to apprehend Blake, Jackson and her group yelled and swore at them and advanced on them, and fights broke out between officers and members of the group. Blake was apprehended. Still more officers arrived, along with help from surrounding agencies.

A fight ensued between a female officer, Davis, and a seventeen year old family friend of Jackson's. Seeing it, Jackson, in her own words, ran to interfere with the officer. Her hair was then sprayed with a chemical irritant. She did not know which officer sprayed her, but she testified that the officers had warned everyone in advance that an irritant would be used if she and her group did not disperse.

Jackson was arrested for failure to disperse. She says she asked Officer Pratt to let her get down on her own because of back and shoulder injuries, got to her knees and leaned down, and Pratt pushed her the rest of the way, put his knee on her back and handcuffed her. She says she was roughly lifted and put in a patrol car. Handcuffed in the car, she argued with Officer Davis about the teenager's treatment; Davis started the engine in ninety degree heat, rolled up the windows and said she would see what she could do to adjust Jackson's attitude. The irritant ran from her hair into her eyes and ears. Within minutes, at Jackson's request, Davis sprayed her with water to remove it; three to five minutes passed between the windows going up and the water. At the station Jackson noticed pain and swelling in her little finger, which was diagnosed as fractured; she claims permanent damage. Five people were arrested, and all five, including Jackson, were convicted of misdemeanors.

Jackson sued nine officers, the city and the chief under section 1983 and state tort law. The district court granted summary judgment to all defendants.
holding:
Affirmed. The court applied the two step sequence the Supreme Court had just set out in Saucier v. Katz and found no constitutional violation at the first step.

Nature of the intrusion. Jackson claimed three intrusions: the chemical irritant before her arrest, being pushed to the ground and roughly lifted during handcuffing, and the closed, heated patrol car used to adjust her attitude. Taking her version as true, the court held the intrusions were minimal. Her hair was sprayed after she interfered with Officer Davis's effort to arrest another member of her party. She then alleged injury during what she herself admitted was a normal handcuffing procedure. In the car she kept arguing, the windows were rolled up, the irritant dripped onto her face, and Davis tended to her with water on request within three to five minutes. The court contrasted Headwaters, where pepper spray was applied to protesters' eyelids with swabs and sprayed into their faces from inches away.

Governmental interest. The interest began with the arrest of Blake on an outstanding felony warrant. As he fled, officers who were substantially outnumbered faced a group that refused commands to disperse, shouted at them, and engaged them in verbal and physical altercations. The safety interest increased further when the group was warned that a chemical irritant would be used if they did not move back and the group refused. Jackson heard the warning, ignored it, and began to directly interfere with Officer Davis's attempt to maintain order. Her active interference posed an immediate threat to the officers' personal safety and their ability to control the group. In circumstances Jackson herself described as a melee, the force applied was reasonable and necessary to control a rapidly evolving and escalating situation. The court rejected her argument that there was no evidence her family and friends had threatened officers or breached the peace, finding that her own testimony contradicted it. Balancing under Graham, the force was not excessive and no Fourth Amendment violation occurred, so summary judgment for the officers was proper.

Qualified immunity. Because there was no violation, the court did not reach Saucier's second step. In a footnote it added that even if the force were excessive, Jackson had not shown that using chemical irritants to overcome resistance to a lawful arrest violated a clearly established right, and a reasonable officer could properly believe this level of force would not do so.

Municipal and supervisory liability. Neither a municipality nor a supervisor can be liable under section 1983 where no constitutional violation occurred (City of Los Angeles v. Heller). The claims against the city and the chief, based on an alleged informal custom of excessive force in emergencies, were properly rejected.

The court also noted, in a footnote, that reasonableness is often a jury question but may be decided as a matter of law when, with all factual disputes resolved for the plaintiff, the force was objectively reasonable. Another footnote distinguished Headwaters on its facts and posture, observed that the Ninth Circuit's section 1983 analysis used there had been rejected in Saucier, and declined to decide whether Headwaters remained good law.
notDecided:
Whether the officers would have had qualified immunity if the force had been excessive. The court did not reach the second Saucier step, and its footnote on the point is an alternative observation, not the holding.

Whether Headwaters remained good law after Saucier. The court expressly declined to decide that; the Headwaters panel later reaffirmed its result on remand.

Whether Officer Mendiola drew his weapon or whether doing so was unreasonable. Jackson did not witness it and the court held she could not assert that claim.

How Jackson's finger was fractured. The court noted the injury and her claim of permanent damage but did not attribute it to any particular act.

Any broader rule about chemical agents on crowds. The holding rests on the specific facts: an outnumbered force, a fleeing arrestee, a group that fought and ignored a dispersal warning, and a plaintiff who ran to interfere.
inPractice:
Jackson is the case to pair with Headwaters, because the same tool produced the opposite result for reasons every officer can articulate. In Headwaters the subjects were seated, passive, posed no threat and could be carried out; the officers had planned the spray in advance and had time. In Jackson the officers were outnumbered, the arrestee had fled into a hostile crowd, fights had already broken out, and the plaintiff admitted she ran to interfere with an officer who was fighting a teenager. The court called it a melee and credited the officers' need to control a rapidly evolving situation.

The warning mattered. The group was told that an irritant would be used if they did not move back, the group refused, and the court said that refusal increased the safety interest. Jackson heard the warning and ignored it. A warning that is given and defied strengthens the justification for the force that follows.

The level of force mattered too. The spray reached her hair, not her eyes, and the court described the intrusion as minimal, distinguishing swabs to the eyelids and face blasts from inches away. The push to the ground came during what she admitted was a normal handcuffing procedure. And the irritant was washed off within minutes of her asking. Decontamination on request helped the officers here, just as withholding it hurt the officers in Headwaters.

Finally, the case shows that no violation means no municipal case. Without a constitutional injury at the hands of an officer, a claim that the city had an informal custom of excessive force in emergencies could not proceed.

Dr. Sowards teaches Jackson in the less lethal line as the active interference counterpoint to Headwaters' passive resistance, and as a reminder that the warning before chemical agents is part of what made the force reasonable.
trainIt:
Teach Jackson and Headwaters together. Put the two fact patterns side by side and have students list the Graham differences: threat to officers, number of officers versus subjects, whether the subject was passive or actively interfering, whether the decision was planned or made in a developing scene, whether a warning was given and defied, where the agent was applied and how much, and how quickly decontamination was offered. The exercise teaches the factors better than either case alone.

Train the crowd warning as a tactical step. The court credited the fact that officers warned everyone that an irritant would be used if the group did not disperse. Students should practice a clear, loud, repeated dispersal warning that names the consequence, and should document who gave it, what was said, and how the crowd responded.

Train decontamination on request. Water within minutes of the request was part of why the court found the intrusion minimal. Build decontamination into every chemical agent evolution and into the report.

Teach the handcuffing holding carefully. Jackson asked to go down on her own because of injuries, got to her knees, and was pushed the rest of the way with a knee on her back. The court accepted her description of a normal handcuffing procedure and found it minimal. That does not license ignoring a stated injury; it means that a controlled assist to the ground during a chaotic arrest, with no gratuitous force, was within the range of reasonable. Train students to hear and note the subject's statement and to use only the control needed.

Teach the patrol car conduct as a caution, not a model. Rolling up the windows in ninety degree heat with a comment about adjusting her attitude was part of the record. The court found the overall intrusion minimal because water followed within minutes, but the comment and the act were plainly not the reason the officers prevailed, and students should not treat them as acceptable.

Teach the posture: summary judgment for the defendants affirmed because the court found no constitutional violation on the plaintiff's own account, with qualified immunity mentioned only as an alternative in a footnote.
caution: The opinion was read from the Public.Resource.Org archive, which has no reporter pagination, so no pin cites are given. The decision was submitted without oral argument. The holding is that no Fourth Amendment violation occurred on Jackson's version of the facts; qualified immunity was discussed only in a footnote as an alternative ground, so the course description of the case as a qualified immunity grant should be understood in that light. The opinion was decided months after Saucier and before the Headwaters remand opinion, and its footnote questioning whether Headwaters remained good law was answered by the Headwaters panel in 2002. The opinion's descriptions of the warrant are inconsistent (a misdemeanor theft conviction in the facts, a felony warrant in the analysis) and the brief reports both.

applications.title: Active interference is an immediate threat
applications.body: Jackson admitted she ran to interfere with an officer who was fighting a teenager during a melee. The court held her active interference posed an immediate threat to the officers' safety and their ability to control the group. That is the fact that separates this case from the passive protesters in Headwaters.

applications.title: A warning that is defied strengthens the justification
applications.body: Officers warned everyone that a chemical irritant would be used if the group did not move back, and the group refused. The court said the safety interest increased further at that point. Give the warning, document it, and note the response.

applications.title: Where and how much
applications.body: Spray that landed in the hair of an interfering person was a minimal intrusion. The court contrasted swabs to closed eyelids and full blasts to the face from inches away. The same tool is judged by the amount and the manner of its use.

applications.title: Decontaminate on request
applications.body: Water within three to five minutes of her request was part of why the intrusion was minimal. Relief after exposure is part of the force analysis and it cut in the officers' favor here.

applications.title: No violation, no municipal case
applications.body: Because no constitutional violation occurred, the claims against the city and the chief based on an alleged custom of excessive force in emergencies failed under City of Los Angeles v. Heller.

applications.title: Posture
applications.body: Summary judgment for all defendants was affirmed on the plaintiff's own version of the facts. The court found the force objectively reasonable and did not reach qualified immunity except in an alternative footnote. The conduct in the patrol car was part of the record but was not the basis of the ruling.

quiz.q: What fact did the court rely on most heavily in finding that the use of the chemical irritant on Jackson was reasonable?
options: That she was drinking in the park
That she ran to interfere with an officer during a melee, after the group had been warned to disperse or face a chemical irritant, posing an immediate threat to officer safety and control
That her son had a warrant
That she was later convicted of a misdemeanor
quiz.teach: The court described outnumbered officers, a fleeing arrestee, a group that shouted, swore, advanced and fought, a warning that was refused, and a plaintiff who by her own account ran to interfere. Her active interference was the immediate threat.

quiz.q: How did the court distinguish Jackson from Headwaters Forest Defense?
options: It did not; it overruled Headwaters

Headwaters involved a small group of passive demonstrators in lock down devices, pepper spray applied to the eyelids and face instead of removing the devices, and a different procedural posture, while Jackson involved spray in the hair of a person actively interfering during a melee
Jackson involved a felony and Headwaters did not
quiz.teach: The court's footnote stressed the passive conduct of the Headwaters protesters, the repeated applications to eyes and faces, and the fact that Headwaters reviewed a directed verdict and did not decide whether the force was excessive. It declined to decide whether Headwaters remained good law after Saucier.

quiz.q: On what ground did the court affirm summary judgment for the officers?
options: Qualified immunity because the law was unclear
That no Fourth Amendment violation occurred because, on Jackson's own version of the facts, the force was objectively reasonable
That Jackson consented to the force
That the city had a lawful policy
quiz.teach: Applying Saucier's first step, the court found the force reasonable and so did not reach the clearly established question, which it mentioned only in a footnote as an alternative. Because there was no violation, the municipal and supervisory claims failed as well.
